Maladaptive Strategies.value: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Marcus had been walking to his car after closing the restaurant kitchen when the engine roared behind him. The headlights cut through the alley, followed by the heavy thud of a door hitting pavement. Before he could step back, a hand yanked his shoulder, twisting his arm against his ribs. He was forced into the backseat of an idling sedan, the smell of stale tobacco and burnt rubber filling his lungs. Hands pinned his wrists. Words were shouted, sharp and relentless, and then the violence began. He fought until his muscles burned, but the weight on top of him never shifted. He remember the steering wheel grinding under his hip, the tires screeching as they tore through a red light. He had felt his body surrender to a force he could not stop, every instinct to resist crushed by the sheer impossibility of it. In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself pacing the perimeter of his apartment, eyes fixed on the peephole long after the deadbolt clicked. He was certain that safety was a temporary arrangement, one that could be broken by a single loose window or a car idling too close to the curb. When delivery drivers revved their engines outside, his chest tightened until his breath came in shallow pulls. He would stand in the center of his kitchen, scanning his own arms and legs for bruises, for tears in his skin, for any sign that the attack had left something behind. The checking became ritual. If he missed a patch of skin, his hands moved faster, driven by a quiet terror that the danger might still be attached to him. Alongside the scanning, he kept a quiet ledger in his mind, replaying scenes where he turned the tables, where the power shifted and the ones who had done this would finally feel the weight they had forced upon him. Back on the line, the heat of the pass and the rhythm of service became a fragile armor. He preferred the back corner of the prep station, away from the swinging service doors. When a sous chef lunged forward to grab a pan, Marcus flinched so hard he dropped a knife into the drain. Sudden movements still put him on guard, his shoulders locking before his brain could register that it was only Marcus swapping out a gas line. He learned to leave the restaurant through the alley entrance, avoiding the street where the traffic always seemed to pause just long enough to make his pulse spike. He started timing his breaks, counting the seconds between the exhaust notes of passing vehicles, waiting for the false alarms to subside. Some nights, he sat in his truck for twenty minutes after shifting into park, listening to the engine tick as it cooled, certain that stillness was the only safe option. When friends asked what had happened, he would open his mouth and watch the words scatter. He tried to explain the event, but the thread always slipped from his fingers, leaving him grasping at half-formed phrases until he shut his mouth and looked away. In his head, the voices from those nights returned without warning, crisp and undeniable, layered over the smell of his own fear. He had come to believe that nobody would have intervened, that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening if they had been there, and that the way he had held still, the way he had fought and then stopped, meant he had acted in ways that went against who he is. He detached himself from the memories as they came, letting them wash over him like static, refusing to let them take root in the present. What frightened him most was the quiet certainty that he had no future, only a series of days to survive. He came to the clinic because the kitchen had become impossible. The constant scanning, the sudden jolts at unexpected sounds, the way he watched his own reflection in the pass-through window as if expecting someone to step through it, had finally caught up with him. He sat in the waiting room tracing the edge of his coffee cup, hoping the person behind the desk might finally see the danger without needing him to describe it, though he was terrified that speaking the truth would make it real all over again.
